## The incident

Spinach is rich in iron, the story goes, because somebody put a decimal point in the wrong place. Hamblin's 1981 article in the BMJ's Christmas issue states it as settled. He dates the original measurement to the 1890s and says German chemists showed in the 1930s that the original workers had overstated its iron by a factor of 10. "Spinach is no better for you than cabbage, Brussels sprouts, or broccoli," he concludes.

Rekdal finds the claim earlier, in a 1972 inaugural lecture by Bender at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London.

## Who lied

Bender hedged. The fame of spinach, he said, "may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point."

Hamblin stated the German correction without a source. His passage carries no citation, and Sutton counts 13 references in the whole article, none of which cites the decimal error or the 1930s Germans.

Sutton reports that Hamblin, in an email, said he had been asked by the BMJ's editor for a humorous Christmas piece, and had been asked not to provide references. Hamblin, Sutton reports, closed by saying he was "sure that he had not made it up."

## The bit continues

Sutton read the Thimble Theatre strips from 1928 to 1935. In the strip of 3 July 1932, the first in which Popeye explains why he eats spinach, the credit goes to vitamin A. "Segar chose and promoted spinach for its vitamin A content alone," Sutton writes.

Sutton also quotes a 2009 chemistry book on the 1890 measurement, which was made on dried spinach: "Wherever lies the truth, the error was not picked up until 1937."

The textbook example of an uncorrected error has no traceable source. It was retold by writers warning about bad citation. Larsson's 1995 paper, "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation," repeated the story and cited Hamblin.

## The incident

In December 1981 the BMJ's Christmas issue carried T. J. Hamblin's "Fake!", an article on "frauds, hoaxes, fakes, and widely popularised mistakes". It said spinach's reputation as an iron source rested on an error. The original workers, in the 1890s, put the decimal point in the wrong place, and German chemists in the 1930s found a 10-fold overestimate. The paragraph has no citation. The article ends with 13 references. Sutton counts none of them as citing the decimal error or the 1930s Germans.

The story predates him. In a 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London, Bender wrote that "the fame of spinach may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point." Rekdal finds "a large number of apparently independent sources" that have "mutually confirmed" the error, whether it was made "in 1870, in the 1890s, or in the 1930s." Larsson's 1995 paper repeated it, citing Hamblin.

## Who lied

The record is hedges, omissions and repetition. Bender hedged. Hamblin stated the figure without a source. Sutton reports Hamblin's reply to his email. Hamblin wrote that he had been asked about this before and that he "honestly cannot remember" it. He said the BMJ's editor had asked him for a humorous Christmas piece and had asked him not to provide references. He was, Sutton reports, "sure that he had not made it up."

## The bit continues

Sutton read the bound volumes of the Thimble Theatre strips from 1928 to 1935. The strip of 3 July 1932, the first in which Popeye explains why he eats spinach, credits vitamin A. Of the "hundreds of Popeye cartoons" he studied, none links spinach to iron. "In fact, Segar chose and promoted spinach for its vitamin A content alone."

The measurement is disputed as well. An account Sutton quotes says the high figure came from dried spinach. He cites dried-spinach measurements of 44.8 mg and about 34 mg per 100 g. If that account is right, the figure measured something other than fresh spinach.

The story is offered as the classic example of an uncorrected error, and it has no traceable source. Several of the people who retold it were writing about accuracy and citation. Rekdal's line on them: "By using the non-existent, or at least undocumented, decimal point error as an illustration of the importance of accuracy and critical investigation, Bender, Hamblin, Larsson, and Skrabanek and McCormick all end up doing the opposite of what they are preaching."

## The incident

In its Christmas issue of 19 December 1981, the BMJ published "Fake!" by T.J. Hamblin, an article about "Frauds, hoaxes, fakes, and widely popularised mistakes". A paragraph covered spinach: "German chemists reinvestigating the iron content of spinach had shown in the 1930s that the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate of its value." For iron, it added, Popeye "would have been better off chewing the cans."

The paragraph has no citation. The article ends with 13 publications Hamblin would "particularly like to mention". In 2010 Mike Sutton, Reader in Criminology at Nottingham Trent University, counted the same 13: "none of which, however, cite the source of the decimal error or 1930's Germans".

## Who lied

Nobody, on the record. The story predates the article. Rekdal (2014) reports a 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London, in which Bender said "the fame of spinach may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point." Bender hedged. Kronick, in 1985, also hedged: "It has been suggested." Hamblin stated it as fact.

Sutton emailed Hamblin. Sutton reports that Hamblin "honestly cannot remember", that the BMJ's then editor had asked him for a humorous Christmas piece and "asked not to provide references", and that he "was sure that he had not made it up."

The tellings do not agree on when the error happened. Rekdal: sources "mutually confirmed the 'fact' that a decimal point error was made, whether it was in 1870, in the 1890s, or in the 1930s." Sutton asked: "Who is von Wolff and where are his erroneous findings recorded?" His references list von Wolff's 1871 Aschen-analysen. No source here produces the page with the misplaced decimal point.

Sutton quotes a second version, from a 2009 Royal Society of Chemistry book by Coultate: von Bunge in 1890 found 35 mg of iron per 100 g, but had analysed dried spinach. Dried spinach has since measured 44.8 mg (Jackson 1938) and about 34 mg (Oladele and Obarisaide 2009). USDA lists raw spinach at 2.71 mg. The high figure may be a correct measurement of a different food.

Also: Popeye. Sutton read the Thimble Theatre strips from 1928 to 1935. In the strip of 3 July 1932, the first in which Popeye explains his spinach, the reason is vitamin A. In "hundreds of Popeye cartoons studied", Sutton found none linking spinach to iron.

## The bit continues

In 1995 Larsson published "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation" in the Journal of Internal Medicine. It repeated the spinach story, citing Hamblin. Rekdal: "Larsson obviously has an important message, but he manages to do exactly what he is criticizing others for in quite a spectacular way."

Rekdal opens his own paper by citing Larsson for the story. Later he discloses the method: "In short, I have plagiarized the Hamblin reference from Larsson." It was a demonstration.

runs.body:
## The incident

The BMJ's Christmas issue of 19 December 1981 carried "Fake!", an article by T.J. Hamblin on "Frauds, hoaxes, fakes, and widely popularised mistakes". A single paragraph covered spinach. The discovery that it was "as valuable a source of iron as red meat" was made in the 1890s, he wrote, but "German chemists reinvestigating the iron content of spinach had shown in the 1930s that the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate of its value." His conclusion: "For a source of iron Popeye would have been better off chewing the cans."

The paragraph has no citation. The article ends with 13 publications Hamblin says he would "particularly like to mention". In 2010 Sutton, a Reader in Criminology at Nottingham Trent University, counted them: "none of which, however, cite the source of the decimal error or 1930's Germans".

## Who lied

Nobody, on the record. The story is older than Hamblin's paragraph. In a 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London, Bender said "the fame of spinach may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point". A 1985 version by Kronick kept the hedge: "It has been suggested." Hamblin's version stated it as fact.

Sutton emailed Hamblin. Sutton reports that Hamblin "honestly cannot remember" the source, that the BMJ's then editor had asked him for "a humorous piece" and asked him "not to provide references", and that Hamblin "was sure that he had not made it up."

Sutton also quotes a 2009 Royal Society of Chemistry book by Coultate, which offers 2 versions. Either von Bunge found 35 mg of iron per 100 g in 1890 but had analysed dried spinach, or a chemist about 20 years earlier misplaced the decimal point. "Wherever lies the truth, the error was not picked up until 1937". Raw spinach, per the USDA: 2.71 mg per 100 g.

Sutton read the Thimble Theatre strips from 1928 to 1935. He reports that the strip of 3 July 1932, the first in which Popeye explains why he eats spinach, credits vitamin A, and that none of the "hundreds of Popeye cartoons studied" links spinach to iron.

## The bit continues

In 1995 Larsson published "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation" in the Journal of Internal Medicine. It repeats the spinach story, citing Hamblin. Rekdal (2014): "Larsson obviously has an important message, but he manages to do exactly what he is criticizing others for in quite a spectacular way."

Rekdal opens his own paper by citing Larsson, then explains, as a deliberate demonstration: "In short, I have plagiarized the Hamblin reference from Larsson."

The tellings do not agree on when the error happened. Rekdal: "a large number of apparently independent sources have mutually confirmed the 'fact' that a decimal point error was made, whether it was in 1870, in the 1890s, or in the 1930s."

original.body:
## The incident

In the BMJ's 1981 Christmas issue, T.J. Hamblin published "Fake!", a survey of "Frauds, hoaxes, fakes, and widely popularised mistakes". 1 paragraph covered spinach: "German chemists reinvestigating the iron content of spinach had shown in the 1930s that the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate of its value." It closed: "For a source of iron Popeye would have been better off chewing the cans."

The paragraph carries no citation. The article ends with 13 publications it was "derived from". None is about spinach.

Raw spinach holds 2.71 mg of iron per 100 g, by the USDA's count. Sutton cites a 1938 measurement of dried spinach at 44.8 mg. A 2009 textbook by Coultate, as Sutton quotes it, offers 2 versions: von Bunge found 35 mg per 100 g in 1890 but had analysed dried spinach, or von Wolf misplaced the decimal point about 20 years earlier. The famous figure may be a correct measurement of a different thing.

## Who lied

Nobody, on the record available. The earliest version Rekdal found is Bender's 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, London: "the fame of spinach may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point." Kronick in 1985 also hedged: "It has been suggested." Hamblin's version dropped the hedge and added the German chemists.

Mike Sutton, a Reader in Criminology at Nottingham Trent University, emailed Hamblin. Sutton reports that Hamblin "honestly cannot remember", that the BMJ's then editor had asked him for a humorous Christmas piece and asked him "not to provide references", and that Hamblin was "sure that he had not made it up."

Sutton's questions included "Who is von Wolff and where are his erroneous findings recorded?" After weeks of searching he could not answer it. He also read the Thimble Theatre strips from 1928 to 1935. In the strip of 3 July 1932, the first in which Popeye explains his spinach, he credits vitamin A. Sutton's conclusion: "Segar chose and promoted spinach for its vitamin A content alone."

The tellings also disagree on the year. Rekdal: sources had "mutually confirmed the 'fact' that a decimal point error was made, whether it was in 1870, in the 1890s, or in the 1930s."

## The bit continues

In 1995 the Journal of Internal Medicine published Larsson's "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation". It repeated the spinach story, citing Hamblin. Rekdal: "Larsson obviously has an important message, but he manages to do exactly what he is criticizing others for in quite a spectacular way."

Rekdal's own 2014 paper, "Academic urban legends", opens by citing Larsson for the story, then stops: "In short, I have plagiarized the Hamblin reference from Larsson." The demonstration was deliberate. It is the only telling in this exhibit that announces its own citation chain.
